questions.stem: What is the principal mechanism of action of OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral)?

choices.text: Relaxes prostate and urethral smooth muscle
choices.explanation: Alpha-1A/alpha-1D antagonism reduces bladder-neck and prostatic smooth-muscle tone, easing urinary flow.

choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 50S subunit
choices.explanation: This is a different pharmacological action. The drug’s action is: Alpha-1A/alpha-1D antagonism reduces bladder-neck and prostatic smooth-muscle tone, easing urinary flow.

choices.text: Reduces vagal bronchoconstriction
choices.explanation: This is a different pharmacological action. The drug’s action is: Alpha-1A/alpha-1D antagonism reduces bladder-neck and prostatic smooth-muscle tone, easing urinary flow.

choices.text: Increases renal glucose and sodium excretion
choices.explanation: This is a different pharmacological action. The drug’s action is: Alpha-1A/alpha-1D antagonism reduces bladder-neck and prostatic smooth-muscle tone, easing urinary flow.

questions.point: Identify the principal pharmacological action taught for this medicine.

questions.stem: Which drug class does OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral) belong to?

choices.text: Alpha/beta blocker
choices.explanation: The medicine is classified as: Selective alpha-1A/alpha-1D adrenergic receptor blocker (uroselective alpha-blocker).

choices.text: Dihydropyridine CCB
choices.explanation: The medicine is classified as: Selective alpha-1A/alpha-1D adrenergic receptor blocker (uroselective alpha-blocker).

choices.text: Uroselective alpha-1 blocker
choices.explanation: Selective alpha-1A/alpha-1D adrenergic receptor blocker (uroselective alpha-blocker).

choices.text: Non-dihydropyridine CCB
choices.explanation: The medicine is classified as: Selective alpha-1A/alpha-1D adrenergic receptor blocker (uroselective alpha-blocker).

questions.point: Identify the drug class taught for this medicine.

questions.stem: Which is a clinical use of OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral)?

choices.text: Treatment of susceptible bacterial infection
choices.explanation: This is a different treatment role.

choices.text: Replacement of circulating glucose in severe hypoglycemia
choices.explanation: This is a different treatment role.

choices.text: Relief of lower urinary tract symptoms caused by benign prostatic hyperplasia
choices.explanation: This is a clinical use of the medicine: Relieves lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), such as weak urinary stream, hesitancy and incomplete emptying. In an ED, alpha-blockers including tamsulosin may also be prescribed OFF-LABEL as medical expulsive therapy (MET) for selected uncomplicated distal ureteral stones, particularly 5–10 mm, after clinician assessment. Not a treatment for sepsis or an infected obstructed urinary system.

choices.text: Acute reversal of opioid respiratory toxicity
choices.explanation: This is a different treatment role.

questions.point: Identify the main treatment role taught for this medicine.

questions.stem: A patient becomes light-headed on standing after OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral). Which paired assessment best checks the suspected adverse effect?

choices.text: Bowel frequency and abdominal distension
choices.explanation: These investigate a gastrointestinal effect rather than postural circulatory tolerance.

choices.text: Resting temperature and infection symptoms
choices.explanation: These investigate infection rather than the suspected pressure effect.

choices.text: Visual acuity and accommodation symptoms
choices.explanation: These evaluate visual effects rather than establish a postural pressure fall.

choices.text: Postural BP and associated symptoms
choices.explanation: A positional pressure fall can account for the light-headedness.

questions.point: Recognize symptomatic hypotension during treatment.

questions.stem: A patient taking OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral) reports dizziness on standing. What is the priority nursing assessment?

choices.text: Blood glucose alone
choices.explanation: Glucose does not assess the suspected drug-related positional pressure drop.

choices.text: Sitting and standing BP with symptoms
choices.explanation: Alpha-1 blockade may cause orthostatic hypotension; a safe posture and BP/symptom reassessment help identify risk.

choices.text: Respiratory rate at rest only
choices.explanation: This does not directly assess orthostatic symptoms.

choices.text: Daily temperature trend
choices.explanation: Temperature does not establish postural hemodynamic effects.

questions.point: Prevent postural hypotension, syncope and falls with alpha-1-blocker therapy.

questions.stem: A patient taking OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral) is scheduled for cataract surgery. Which information is important to communicate?

choices.text: Current or past tamsulosin exposure
choices.explanation: Tamsulosin is linked with intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery.

choices.text: Whether the patient uses paracetamol
choices.explanation: This is not the main medication-specific concern.

choices.text: Timing of the patient's last meal only
choices.explanation: Fasting requirements do not address iris effects.

choices.text: History of seasonal allergies only
choices.explanation: This does not address the drug-specific operative issue.

questions.point: Notify the eye surgeon about current or previous tamsulosin use before cataract surgery.

questions.stem: Besides benign prostate symptoms, what is a selected emergency-department use of OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral)?

choices.text: Dissolving bladder infection bacteria
choices.explanation: Tamsulosin is not an antibiotic.

choices.text: Stopping gastrointestinal hemorrhage
choices.explanation: It has no hemostatic action.

choices.text: Rapidly relieving pulmonary edema
choices.explanation: It is not a diuretic or pulmonary-edema rescue medication.

choices.text: Helping passage of distal ureteral stones
choices.explanation: Medical expulsive therapy is an off-label use for carefully selected distal ureteral stones.

questions.point: Recognize selected distal ureteric stones as an off-label ED use of tamsulosin.

questions.stem: A patient prescribed OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral) for a ureteral stone has fever and signs of sepsis. What is the safest nursing response?

choices.text: Encourage ambulation as the only intervention
choices.explanation: Mobility does not address a urological sepsis emergency.

choices.text: Urgently escalate suspected infected obstruction
choices.explanation: Sepsis with an obstructed kidney requires prompt resuscitation, antibiotics and urologic decompression.

choices.text: Rely on stone-expulsive therapy
choices.explanation: Alpha blockers do not treat infection or decompress an obstructed system.

choices.text: Wait for the stone to pass before calling
choices.explanation: Delay in infected obstruction can cause rapid deterioration.

questions.point: Recognize that infected urinary obstruction is an emergency and not managed by tamsulosin alone.

questions.stem: A patient starts OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral) and becomes faint while walking to the bathroom. What should the nurse do first?

choices.text: Give the next dose immediately
choices.explanation: The next dose is not the immediate response to faintness.

choices.text: Increase fluid intake without assessment
choices.explanation: Fluid may be relevant but cannot replace immediate safety assessment.

choices.text: Assist to a safe position and assess BP
choices.explanation: Support the patient and assess for symptomatic hypotension before further therapy.

choices.text: Encourage independent walking
choices.explanation: Walking unaided risks fall injury with syncope.

questions.point: Prevent postural hypotension, syncope and falls with alpha-1-blocker therapy.

questions.stem: A patient stopped OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral) months before planned cataract surgery. What should the nurse still ensure?

choices.text: Restarting the alpha blocker now
choices.explanation: Restarting treatment does not prevent operative iris problems.

choices.text: The ophthalmologist knows the prior treatment
choices.explanation: Past exposure can remain clinically relevant to cataract surgery planning.

choices.text: Changing to an injectable route
choices.explanation: Tamsulosin is an oral drug and this would not address the issue.

choices.text: No disclosure because treatment ended
choices.explanation: IFIS has been reported with prior use.

questions.point: Notify the eye surgeon about current or previous tamsulosin use before cataract surgery.

questions.stem: For which ureteral-stone presentation does guidance most support an alpha blocker like OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral)?

choices.text: An uncomplicated distal stone of 5–10 mm
choices.explanation: EAU 2026 particularly supports alpha blockers for distal ureteral stones 5–10 mm when conservative management is appropriate.

choices.text: Bilateral obstruction with renal impairment
choices.explanation: Renal impairment with obstruction demands urgent evaluation.

choices.text: Uncontrolled pain despite analgesia
choices.explanation: Uncontrolled pain requires escalation, not expulsive therapy alone.

choices.text: Sepsis with obstructed infected kidney
choices.explanation: Infected obstruction requires urgent decompression and antibiotics.

questions.point: Recognize selected distal ureteric stones as an off-label ED use of tamsulosin.

questions.stem: A patient with an obstructing ureteral stone receiving OMNIC — tamsulosin (oral) develops anuria and worsening renal function. What changes the plan?

choices.text: Using the medicine as immediate analgesia
choices.explanation: Tamsulosin is not a rapid pain-relief agent.

choices.text: The need for urgent obstruction evaluation
choices.explanation: New anuria and renal deterioration are urgent warning signs, not indications for MET alone.

choices.text: Increasing dosage without review
choices.explanation: Dose escalation does not resolve dangerous urinary obstruction.

choices.text: Continuing unchanged home therapy
choices.explanation: Worsening obstruction or renal failure requires escalation.

questions.point: Recognize that infected urinary obstruction is an emergency and not managed by tamsulosin alone.

choices.text: Activates plasminogen to break down fibrin
choices.explanation: Alteplase promotes fibrin breakdown; it is distinct from preventing new coagulation.

choices.text: Bronchodilation with a narrow therapeutic index
choices.explanation: This is a different pharmacological action. The drug’s action is: Alteplase promotes fibrin breakdown; it is distinct from preventing new coagulation.

choices.explanation: This is a different pharmacological action. The drug’s action is: Alteplase promotes fibrin breakdown; it is distinct from preventing new coagulation.

choices.explanation: Fibrinolytic/thrombolytic; recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA).

choices.explanation: The medicine is classified as: Fibrinolytic/thrombolytic; recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA).

questions.stem: Which is a clinical use of Alteplase (tPA)?

choices.text: Replacement of glucose during severe hypoglycemia
choices.explanation: This is a different treatment role.

choices.text: Relief of bronchospasm through airway receptor stimulation
choices.explanation: This is a different treatment role.

choices.text: Suppression of bacterial protein synthesis
choices.explanation: This is a different treatment role.

choices.text: Indication-specific emergency thrombolysis in eligible patients
choices.explanation: This is a clinical use of the medicine: Emergency thrombolytic used in eligible acute ischemic stroke; current Activase labeling also includes acute myocardial infarction and acute massive pulmonary embolism. Current 2026 AHA/ASA stroke guidance includes alteplase as an IV thrombolytic option for eligible adults within the 4.5-hour treatment window; selected later/unknown-onset cases require advanced-imaging selection.

questions.point: Identify the main treatment role taught for this medicine.

questions.stem: Why must an alteplase prescription identify whether the indication is stroke, MI, or PE?

choices.text: The full vial defines the same dose across indications
choices.explanation: Container content is not a universal patient dose.

choices.text: Body weight alone defines the schedule across indications
choices.explanation: Weight does not replace the indication-specific regimen.

choices.text: Dose and delivery schedule differ by indication
choices.explanation: The indication-specific regimen must match the authorized order.

choices.text: The generic drug name defines the schedule without the indication
choices.explanation: A shared drug name does not establish the same regimen.

questions.point: Alteplase regimens differ by indication.

questions.stem: For acute ischemic stroke treated with IV alteplase, what percentage of the total dose is given as the initial bolus?
questions.explanation: The regimen gives 10% initially and the remainder by infusion.
questions.point: The initial stroke bolus is 10% of the total dose.

questions.stem: For acute ischemic stroke treated with IV alteplase, over how many minutes is the remainder infused after the initial bolus?
questions.explanation: The remainder is infused over 60 minutes in the quoted regimen.
questions.point: The remainder of the taught stroke regimen infuses over 60 minutes.

questions.stem: During Alteplase (tPA) therapy, a patient has new melena, pallor, dizziness, and a BP fall. Which concern best unifies the findings?

choices.text: Isolated vasodilator headache
choices.explanation: This does not explain melena and the systemic blood-loss pattern.

choices.text: Uncomplicated postural intolerance
choices.explanation: This does not account for the new evidence of GI bleeding.

choices.text: Clinically important blood loss
choices.explanation: The stool finding and hemodynamic change suggest bleeding with impaired perfusion.

choices.text: A therapeutic reduction in coagulation alone
choices.explanation: Bleeding with circulatory symptoms is more than evidence of the intended drug action.

questions.point: Recognize important bleeding during antithrombotic treatment.

questions.stem: Before alteplase for a suspected ischemic stroke, which completed assessment is essential to the eligibility decision?

choices.text: A normal temperature without brain imaging
choices.explanation: Temperature does not distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.

choices.text: A low pain score without brain imaging
choices.explanation: Pain severity does not establish thrombolysis eligibility.

choices.text: A normal peripheral pulse without brain imaging
choices.explanation: Pulse assessment does not exclude intracranial bleeding.

choices.text: Brain imaging excluding hemorrhage with protocol eligibility review
choices.explanation: Stroke symptoms alone do not establish suitability for thrombolysis.

questions.point: Exclude intracranial hemorrhage and verify eligibility before stroke thrombolysis.

questions.stem: During alteplase, sudden severe headache, vomiting, and neurological worsening occur. Which complication is the priority to exclude?

choices.text: Intracranial hemorrhage
choices.explanation: This is a major thrombolysis complication requiring immediate escalation and emergency assessment.

choices.text: A routine migraine episode
choices.explanation: The treatment context and acute neurological change require urgent exclusion of hemorrhage rather than assuming a benign headache.

choices.text: An uncomplicated therapeutic response
choices.explanation: Neurological deterioration is not a sign of successful treatment.

choices.text: An isolated local infusion reaction
choices.explanation: A local site problem does not explain this neurological cluster.

questions.point: Acute neurological worsening during thrombolysis needs immediate escalation.

questions.stem: The Activase label states a 3-hour stroke window, while current AHA/ASA guidance supports selected eligible patients within 4.5 hours. What must guide a time-sensitive treatment decision?

choices.text: The assumption that any later presentation automatically qualifies
choices.explanation: Later or unknown-onset cases require specific selection criteria.

choices.text: The assumption that symptom severity alone establishes eligibility
choices.explanation: Time, imaging, contraindications, and the protocol remain relevant.

choices.text: The assumption that a treatment window excludes imaging requirements
choices.explanation: Hemorrhage exclusion and eligibility still matter.

choices.text: The newest applicable authorized stroke protocol and eligibility assessment
choices.explanation: The label/guideline distinction must be recognized rather than mixed into an improvised rule.

questions.point: Stroke thrombolysis timing follows current eligibility guidance and local protocol.

questions.stem: A hypothetical 110-kg adult meets the stated stroke protocol eligibility. Using 0.9 mg/kg with a 90-mg maximum, what total dose is calculated? Enter mg.
questions.explanation: 110 × 0.9 = 99 mg before the cap; the maximum limits the total to 90 mg.
questions.point: Apply the taught 0.9 mg/kg stroke dose with 90 mg maximum.

questions.stem: Which BP limits apply immediately before and during the first 24 hours after IV alteplase for acute ischemic stroke?

choices.text: Before: <160/90; afterward: ≤160/90 mm Hg
choices.explanation: These are not the protocol limits.

choices.text: Before: <200/120; afterward: ≤200/120 mm Hg
choices.explanation: These are not the limits.

choices.text: Before: <185/110; afterward: ≤180/105 mm Hg
choices.explanation: These are the pre- and post-treatment limits.

choices.text: Before: <180/105; afterward: ≤185/110 mm Hg
choices.explanation: This reverses the two thresholds.

questions.point: Distinguish pre-treatment BP eligibility from post-thrombolysis limits.

questions.stem: An antiplatelet or anticoagulant is proposed after IV alteplase for acute ischemic stroke. What is required before starting it?

choices.text: Completion of the infusion as the sole clearance criterion
choices.explanation: Finishing the dose does not by itself establish that antithrombotics can start.

choices.text: The authorized post-thrombolysis assessment and follow-up imaging plan
choices.explanation: Bleeding risk and follow-up findings guide the protocol decision.

choices.text: A normal peripheral pulse as the sole clearance criterion
choices.explanation: This does not exclude intracranial bleeding.

choices.text: Improved speech as the sole clearance criterion
choices.explanation: Neurological benefit does not replace the protocol’s imaging requirement.

questions.point: Follow post-thrombolysis monitoring/imaging before antithrombotic treatment.

questions.stem: What defines complete heart block?

choices.text: Uniformly slow sinus impulses that all conduct
choices.explanation: This describes sinus bradycardia rather than complete block.

choices.text: A ventricular rate that must exceed the atrial rate
choices.explanation: This is not the defining relationship.

choices.text: Rapid conduction through every atrial impulse
choices.explanation: This does not describe AV dissociation.

choices.explanation: Atria and ventricles then beat independently.

choices.text: Each P wave followed by one QRS with a fixed PR
choices.explanation: This demonstrates conducted atrial impulses rather than complete block.

choices.explanation: Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms are the hallmark.

choices.text: A continuous absence of all atrial and ventricular signals

choices.text: A normal P/QRS relationship with a fast sinus rate
choices.explanation: This is not complete AV block.

questions.stem: What is the principal role of telemetry?

choices.text: Direct measurement of cardiac output
choices.explanation: The ECG waveform does not directly quantify output.

choices.text: Continuous cardiac electrical rhythm monitoring
choices.explanation: Telemetry follows heart rate and rhythm over time.

choices.text: Replacement of every diagnostic 12-lead assessment
choices.explanation: Continuous rhythm monitoring does not provide the same diagnostic study.

choices.text: Direct measurement of myocardial blood flow
choices.explanation: Telemetry measures electrical activity rather than coronary flow.

choices.text: ECG: urine output; pleth: coronary anatomy

choices.text: ECG: ventricular pressure; pleth: clotting intensity

choices.text: ECG: electrical activity; pleth: pulsatile blood flow

choices.text: ECG: arterial oxygen content; pleth: AV conduction
choices.explanation: This reverses and misidentifies the signal roles.

choices.text: Pain score, wound depth, and drainage volume
choices.explanation: These assess another clinical domain.

choices.text: Bowel frequency, dietary intake, and stool color
choices.explanation: These do not interpret cardiac electrical relationships.

questions.stem: Which intervention is used for VF or pulseless VT arrest?

questions.stem: A patient has an unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse. Which electrical mode usually applies?

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion
choices.explanation: The shock is timed to the R wave in the appropriate pulse-present rhythm.

choices.text: Unsynchronized shock as the rule for every pulse-present rhythm
choices.explanation: This ignores the synchronization requirement and specific exceptions.

choices.text: No electrical treatment until all biomarkers return

questions.stem: Why is a cardioversion shock synchronized to the R wave?

choices.text: To deliver pacing impulses between every pair of QRS complexes
choices.explanation: This describes neither a synchronized shock nor its purpose.

choices.text: To make shock energy depend on the atrial rate
choices.explanation: Synchronization selects timing, not energy based on atrial rate.

choices.text: To avoid shock delivery during vulnerable ventricular repolarization
choices.explanation: This reduces the risk of triggering a dangerous ventricular rhythm.

choices.text: To guarantee a pulse whenever a QRS is detected
choices.explanation: Electrical detection does not guarantee mechanical perfusion.

questions.point: Synchronization avoids the vulnerable repolarization period.

choices.text: An isolated normal ECG with no symptoms

choices.text: VF arrest requiring defibrillation

choices.explanation: A stimulus alone does not establish capture.

choices.text: A pacing spike followed by a QRS complex
choices.explanation: This is electrical capture; the patient still needs a mechanical response check.

questions.point: Electrical capture is a pacing spike followed by a QRS complex.

questions.stem: Why is magnesium relevant when hypokalemia is difficult to correct?

choices.explanation: The prohibition concerns uncontrolled rapid IV administration.

choices.text: Only at the opposite limb without checking the injured side
choices.explanation: Comparison cannot replace assessment of the affected limb.

choices.explanation: This does not assess distal tissue at risk.

choices.explanation: Tissue below the injury may lose blood flow or nerve function.

choices.text: Pain, blood supply, feeling, movement, and swelling
choices.explanation: These cover the neurovascular and pressure concerns.

choices.explanation: These are incomplete for the neurovascular assessment.

questions.stem: What is the central mechanism of acute compartment syndrome?

choices.text: An isolated superficial skin allergy increases every distal pulse
choices.explanation: This does not describe compartment physiology.

choices.text: A normal distal pulse increases compartment space
choices.explanation: A pulse does not establish safe compartment pressure.

choices.text: Pressure within a closed compartment compromises tissue perfusion
choices.explanation: Swelling/bleeding can create an ischemia–edema cycle.

choices.text: A venous cannula removes too much joint fluid
choices.explanation: This is not the mechanism responsible.

questions.point: Raised compartment pressure can reduce perfusion and damage nerve/muscle.

choices.text: Comfort improving with unchanged distal findings
choices.explanation: This does not describe the warning change.

choices.text: An unchanged old scar without new symptoms
choices.explanation: This does not indicate an acute pressure problem.

choices.text: Increasing disproportionate pain worsened by passive stretch

choices.explanation: This does not establish a need for the described fixation system.

questions.stem: Which description correctly defines osteomyelitis?

choices.text: Infection involving bone
choices.explanation: This defines osteomyelitis.

choices.text: Loss of bone mineral density
choices.explanation: Reduced density does not define bone infection.

choices.text: Infection confined to superficial skin
choices.explanation: Superficial skin infection is not osteomyelitis.

choices.text: Inflammation confined to a joint
choices.explanation: This refers to joint involvement rather than bone infection.

questions.point: Osteomyelitis is bone infection with possible blood, contiguous, or direct entry.

questions.stem: Which cluster warrants consideration of deeper bone infection?

choices.text: A normal distal examination without wound symptoms
choices.explanation: This does not establish bone infection.

choices.text: A stable old scar without pain or drainage
choices.explanation: No active warning finding is described.

choices.text: A healed wound with steadily improving comfort
choices.explanation: This does not identify ongoing deeper infection.

choices.text: Persistent deep pain with drainage and poor healing
choices.explanation: These findings raise concern for osteomyelitis.

questions.point: Recognize persistent deep pain, drainage, poor healing, and inflammation.

questions.stem: Which set best supports a nursing report of suspected osteomyelitis deterioration?

choices.explanation: Supply does not establish the clinical condition.

choices.text: A device photograph without a patient assessment
choices.explanation: Appearance alone is incomplete.

choices.text: Vitals, wound drainage, pain trend, and distal findings
choices.explanation: These establish local, systemic, and limb-safety information.

choices.text: A dressing brand and the original appointment date
choices.explanation: These do not describe current severity.

questions.point: Assess vitals, wound/drainage, pain trend, and neurovascular status.

questions.stem: Which treatment pattern addresses established osteomyelitis rather than symptoms alone?

choices.text: A short analgesic course followed by wound observation
choices.explanation: Symptom relief alone does not treat established bone infection.

choices.text: Immobilization alone until the pain resolves
choices.explanation: Protecting the limb does not itself eradicate the infection.

choices.text: Surface cleansing alone until the drainage stops
choices.explanation: Surface care alone does not address infection within bone.

choices.text: An extended antimicrobial plan with possible debridement
choices.explanation: Treatment may require antimicrobial therapy and removal of infected tissue.

questions.point: Treatment may include prolonged antibiotics and surgery/debridement.

questions.stem: Which routes can lead to osteomyelitis?

choices.text: Nearby infection only, without bloodstream or traumatic entry
choices.explanation: This excludes two routes.

choices.text: Bloodstream spread, nearby infection, direct traumatic entry
choices.explanation: These are the three routes.

choices.text: Bloodstream spread only, without local or traumatic entry
choices.explanation: This excludes two routes.

choices.text: Direct traumatic entry only, without bloodstream spread
choices.explanation: This excludes hematogenous and nearby spread.

questions.point: Bone infection may arise through bloodstream, contiguous spread, or direct inoculation.
